checkpoints: The client persists only one number, lastSeq — the highest seq it has rendered — with no need to remember any message's content or timestamp.
On reconnect, the client emits a chat:sync { room, lastSeq } event to the server.
The server answers with a single range query, ZRANGEBYSCORE log:{room} (lastSeq +inf, where (lastSeq is an exclusive lower bound on the sorted-set log.
The exclusive bound guarantees a client holding seq N gets N+1 onward and never re-sees N.

The sorted set returns results already ordered by score, removing client-side re-sorting and timestamp comparison, and eliminating clock skew and out-of-order packet arrival as sources of non-determinism.
The log works because every message was ZADDed with score = seq, turning what-did-I-miss into a pure range query on score rather than a fragile timestamp match.

The client should sync by greater-than-lastSeq rather than demanding exactly-lastSeq-plus-1, because a crash between INCR and ZADD orphans a seq with no matching message, and demanding the exact next seq would hang the client forever whereas the greater-than query simply skips the gap and continues.

Plain Redis pub/sub is at-most-once and fire-and-forget: once PUBLISH returns, Redis has done its job regardless of whether any subscriber was actually there to receive it, with no buffer and no replay.
This is fine for presence or typing indicators where a dropped frame is harmless, but it is not durable chat — an offline recipient's message is simply gone.

The fix is to stop trusting the channel as the source of truth and persist each message to a durable store (a DB table or a Redis Stream) before, or atomically with, the PUBLISH call, so the message survives independently of whether anyone was subscribed at that instant.
Pub/sub stays the fast realtime path for whoever is online right now, while the durable store becomes the actual record of what was sent.
An offline or reconnecting client backfills directly from the store using a lastSeq/timestamp cursor per room, which is deterministic and repeatable no matter how long the client was gone.

Redis Streams is the better foundation when you want no-loss and replay built in natively: consumer groups and per-consumer offsets give durable, replayable delivery as a first-class feature, at the cost of more operational surface than plain pub/sub plus a hand-rolled store.
The trade-off is real: every send now pays an extra durable write before or alongside the pub/sub hop.

Redis itself remains a single point of failure needing cluster/sentinel-style HA regardless of which approach is picked — durability moves the loss risk away from 'recipient was offline' but does not remove the need for Redis to stay up.
Sorting by timestamp breaks because the timestamp is each node's own local clock time, and clocks across nodes are never perfectly in sync (clock skew).

Two different nodes can stamp two messages in the opposite order of what actually happened, so each client sorts to a different result depending on which node it is connected to — there is no shared total order.
The correct fix is a centralized per-room sequencer: Redis INCR on key seq:{room}, handing every accepted message the next monotonically increasing, non-duplicating integer.
Because INCR is atomic and runs on a single Redis, it is the single serialization point every node must go through, replacing each node deciding order on its own clock.
Once messages carry seq instead of a timestamp, both clients sort by seq, so no matter which node they are connected to, they always see the exact same order.
To avoid turning the counter into a system-wide bottleneck, seq:{room} must be namespaced per room — one independent counter per room, trading a little write throughput for a guaranteed total order.
A shared channel forces every node to receive and parse every message of every room, at cost O(node count × message count).
Most of that cost is waste, because a node with no member of the room still has to parse the message then discard it.
The re-shape is sharding by room: give each room its own Redis channel.
Each node subscribes only to the rooms it currently has a local member in.
The result is that a message only reaches the nodes that actually have receivers — fanout breadth equals exactly the number of nodes holding a member, observable via PUBSUB NUMSUB.
This requires reference-counting local members per room, so a node SUBSCRIBEs on the 0→1 transition and UNSUBSCRIBEs on the 1→0 transition.
The cost is that channel count grows with room count — Redis handles it, but it needs monitoring.
BITCOUNT and PFCOUNT answer two different cardinality questions, not the same question twice.

BITCOUNT runs over the presence bitmap and returns the exact number of users online right now; a user's bit is only cleared when their last connection disconnects, so that number falls the instant people leave.

PFCOUNT runs over a HyperLogLog fed by PFADD and estimates how many distinct users have ever appeared within a window; a HyperLogLog has no remove operation, so that estimate only grows and never shrinks back down when a user disconnects.

The two structures solve different cost problems: HyperLogLog buys a fixed ~12 KB footprint at ~0.81% standard error regardless of how many millions of ids were fed in, which is why you don't just keep an exact Set of every distinct visitor (that would grow linearly and get expensive at scale).
The two commands are not interchangeable: drive the 'online now' green dot with BITCOUNT, and 'how many distinct users visited today' with PFCOUNT.
Swapping them produces a number that means the wrong thing: PFCOUNT would over-report current presence by still counting people who logged off hours ago.
BITCOUNT cannot express a cumulative unique count, since it has already forgotten anyone no longer connected.
A correctly working backplane already reaches every socket living on any node — that isn't the failure here.
The real problem sits before a connection is even a real WebSocket: Socket.IO opens with plain HTTP long-polling requests, and only after those succeed does it upgrade to a WebSocket.
Those early HTTP requests carry a session id the server must recognize on every follow-up call.

If the load balancer routes the first request to node-1 and the next request to node-2, node-2 has never heard of that session and answers 'Session ID unknown' — the handshake never completes and the backplane never even gets a chance to route anything.
The fix is sticky sessions: the load balancer hashes by IP or by a cookie so every request from the same client keeps landing on the same node for the whole handshake and the life of the connection.

This is a completely different job from the backplane's: the backplane routes a message between two different clients living on two different nodes, while sticky sessions bind one client to one node so its own requests never get scattered across nodes.
Both are needed — a perfectly healthy backplane with a non-sticky load balancer still drops the handshake before any chat message is ever sent.
One escape hatch is forcing transports: ["websocket"], which skips the long-polling phase entirely, but trades away the fallback for any client on a network that blocks raw WebSocket upgrades.
Core claim: messageId and seq are two identifiers with two different sources and two different jobs — they cannot be merged into one.
messageId is generated by the client once per logical message and is known before sending; it answers "have I already received this?" and drives dedup via SET NX.
seq is issued by Redis INCR only after the server accepts the message; it answers "where does this sit in the room's timeline?" and drives ordering.
Making seq the dedup key is impossible: it would require the client to know seq before sending, but seq is only produced after the server's INCR.

Making messageId the order loses total order, because client-generated ids (a UUID or random string) are not monotonic and have no centralized origin — two clients on two different nodes can generate ids in no particular order, with nothing to say one is "greater than" the other in time.

Both identifiers are mandatory, and that duality is exactly what makes retries safe: the client resends the same messageId after a flaky send, SET NX collapses the duplicate resends into one, while INCR keeps guaranteeing a clean total order for genuinely new messages.

Redis presence tracking that stores a single online/offline bit per user only works correctly when each user has exactly one connection at a time; the moment a user has multiple simultaneous connections (phone and laptop, or two browser tabs), the single bit can no longer represent their true state.

A user's real online status is the union of every connection they currently have open, not a reflection of whichever connection most recently changed state — so a disconnect on one device should only affect the shared bit if it was that user's last remaining connection.

Calling `SETBIT presence:online <userId> 0` unconditionally inside `disconnect()` means the very FIRST disconnect for a user clears the bit, even while other connections for that same user are still alive on other nodes — the correct behavior is for only the LAST disconnect to clear it.

The missing piece is a per-user reference count: without tracking how many live connections a user currently has, `connect()` and `disconnect()` have no way to distinguish 'this was one of several connections' from 'this was the only connection.'

The fix is a per-user connection counter stored in Redis (e.g. `presence:conn:<userId>`), incremented with `INCR` on every `connect()` and decremented with `DECR` on every `disconnect()`, so the counter reflects the total number of live connections across the whole cluster.

The online bit should only be written on the edges of that counter: `SETBIT ... 1` fires solely on the 0-to-1 transition (the first connection appearing), and `SETBIT ... 0` (plus removing the counter key) fires solely on the 1-to-0 transition (the last connection disappearing) — connects and disconnects in between just adjust the count without touching the bit.

The counter must live in shared Redis rather than in either node's local process memory, because a user's connections can land on different nodes behind a load balancer; each node only sees its own in-memory state, so only a value that every node can atomically read and update turns 'does this user have any connection left anywhere in the cluster?' into one race-free, globally consistent answer.

Correctness of the fix can be verified by opening two connections for the same user on two different nodes and confirming the online count stays at 1, closing one connection and confirming the user still shows online, and only seeing the state flip to offline once the very last connection closes.

Redis INCR and SET NX are each individually atomic, but calling INCR before SET NX means every accept() call — including a retry of an already-seen messageId — claims a fresh sequence number before the system ever checks whether the message is a duplicate.

When accept() writes the message into the log (ZADD) right after INCR but before the dedup check runs, a retried message ends up stored twice in the log under two different seq values, even though both writes carry identical content.
SET NX on the dedup key is the only call that actually knows whether a given messageId has already been accepted; it therefore must run and be evaluated before any state-mutating step, not after.

Reordering the operations so SET NX runs first turns accept() into a real gate: a null return means the key already existed, so the handler can load and return the previously stored message immediately, without ever calling INCR or ZADD.
Only the caller for which SET NX succeeds (the first writer) should proceed to INCR and ZADD, which limits seq claiming and log writes to genuinely new messages.

Because SET NX and INCR each remain atomic on the same Redis instance, putting the dedup gate first is enough to guarantee that even concurrent retries of the same messageId consume exactly one seq and produce exactly one log row — the atomicity of the individual commands is not sufficient on its own when their order is wrong.

A regression test for this fix sends the same messageId twice (sequentially and concurrently) and asserts that the per-room seq counter advances exactly once and the log holds exactly one row for that message.

The root cause here is not a wrong choice of Redis command — both INCR and SET NX are correct primitives on their own — it is the sequencing of two correct operations, a distinct class of bug from picking the wrong API.

Calling `this.io.to(payload.room).emit(...)` immediately inside the `chat:send` handler already delivers the message to every socket joined to that room on the local node, before any pub/sub round-trip happens.

Because every node — including the node that received the original `chat:send` — subscribes to the same backplane channel, publishing the envelope causes the origin node's own subscription handler to fire and deliver the identical envelope a second time to sockets it already served directly.

The result is an asymmetric duplicate-delivery bug: clients on the origin node receive the message twice while clients on other nodes receive it only once, which is why it can pass a single-node smoke test and only surfaces once two clients share the same node.

The correct design keeps `chat:send` on a single path: the handler should only publish to the backplane, and delivery to any socket — local or remote — should happen exclusively inside the subscription's message callback, so same-node and cross-node clients share identical code.

Re-adding a direct `emit` call at send time reintroduces exactly the 'is the recipient local or remote?' special case the publish/subscribe backplane exists to remove, splitting one delivery route into two competing ones.

The fix is to delete the `this.io.to(payload.room).emit(...)` line from the handler entirely, keep only the `publish` call, and let the subscriber's callback perform all delivery — stamping fields like `originNode` and `deliveredBy` on the envelope there so the routing hop is provable rather than assumed.

Routing every delivery, even same-node, through the backplane costs one extra round-trip, which is an acceptable trade for eliminating a duplicate-delivery bug and the local/remote branching that caused it.

Correct behavior can be confirmed by connecting two clients to the same node and checking that each receives exactly one `chat:message` per send, then repeating with a client on a different node to confirm it also receives exactly one copy.
